```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(pdmS7)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, error = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8,
  fig.height = 4, dpi = if (nzchar(Sys.getenv("IN_PKGDOWN"))) 110 else 60
)
logger::log_threshold(logger::WARN, namespace = "pdmS7")
pal <- c("#236b83", "#a26421", "#5b8c3a", "#8a3b6b", "#444444")
grey <- "#9aa7b0"
panels <- function(n = 2, right = 0.8) {
  par(mfrow = c(1, n), mar = c(4.6, 5.2, 2.2, right), cex.main = 0.95, mgp = c(3.6, 0.7, 0))
}
legend_in <- function(where, labels, lty = seq_along(labels)) {
  legend(where, labels, col = pal[seq_along(labels)], lty = lty, lwd = 2.5, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
}
# Labels at the right-hand end of each line, nudged apart so they do not overlap.
end_labels <- function(x, ys, labels, log_y = FALSE) {
  y <- if (log_y) log10(ys) else ys
  o <- order(y)
  gap <- diff(par("usr")[3:4]) * 0.06
  for (k in seq_along(o)[-1]) y[o[k]] <- max(y[o[k]], y[o[k - 1]] + gap)
  text(x, if (log_y) 10^y else y, labels, col = pal[seq_along(labels)], pos = 4, cex = 0.8,
       xpd = TRUE)
}
```

A PDM is three choices stacked on each other: how the soil store fills and sheds water, how
water reaches groundwater, and how groundwater drains to the river. Each choice leaves its own
mark on the hydrograph. This article shows those marks, one component at a time, with
everything else held fixed, so you can learn to read a river's record and know which part of
the model it is pointing at.

It is written for training. Each section explains how the option works, compares the options
on the same storms, and ends with **what to look for** in an observed record. The last section
gathers these into a single table. The equations are in [Model equations](model-equations.html),
and the configuration options in [Choosing model components](model-options.html).

```{r diagram, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="The three choices this article compares, in the order water meets them."}
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
box_at <- function(x, y, w, h, label, col, fill = 0.15, cex = 0.8, font = 1) {
  rect(x - w / 2, y - h / 2, x + w / 2, y + h / 2, col = adjustcolor(col, fill), border = col,
       lwd = 1.4)
  text(x, y, label, cex = cex, font = font)
}
arrow <- function(x0, y0, x1, y1, col = "#444444") {
  arrows(x0, y0, x1, y1, length = 0.07, col = col, lwd = 1.3)
}
box_at(0.5, 0.92, 0.5, 0.1, "Rain and evaporation", "#444444", fill = 0.05)
box_at(0.5, 0.66, 0.36, 0.16, "1. Soil store\nhow capacity is spread", pal[1], font = 2)
box_at(0.22, 0.34, 0.26, 0.14, "Surface route\nquick flow", grey)
box_at(0.72, 0.38, 0.3, 0.12, "2. Recharge rule", pal[2], font = 2)
box_at(0.72, 0.16, 0.32, 0.14, "3. Groundwater store\nslow flow", pal[3], font = 2)
box_at(0.36, 0.06, 0.24, 0.09, "River", "#444444", fill = 0.05)
arrow(0.5, 0.87, 0.5, 0.74)
arrow(0.4, 0.58, 0.28, 0.41)
text(0.24, 0.52, "direct runoff", cex = 0.72, col = "#444444")
arrow(0.6, 0.58, 0.68, 0.44)
arrow(0.72, 0.32, 0.72, 0.23)
arrow(0.24, 0.27, 0.32, 0.11)
arrow(0.6, 0.12, 0.48, 0.07)
```

```{r forcing}
# Five storms over 40 days, hourly: a small one on a dry catchment, then a wet spell
n <- 24 * 40
rain <- rep(0, n)
storm <- function(day, mm, hours) {
  rain[24 * day + seq_len(hours)] <<- mm / hours
}
storm(2, 10, 4)
storm(9, 20, 6)
storm(13, 30, 8)
storm(15, 30, 8)
storm(18, 15, 3)
forcing <- data.frame(rain = rain, pet = 0.08)
days <- seq_len(n) / 24
storm_days <- c(2, 9, 13, 15, 18)
```

```{r year}
# A year of hourly rain with seasonal evaporation, for the comparisons that need one
year_rain <- synthetic_rain("2020-10-01", years = 1, dt = 1, seed = 3)
year <- data.frame(time = year_rain$time, rain = year_rain$rain, pet = year_rain$pet)
ny <- nrow(year)
# Each model runs the year twice and keeps the second, so its stores start as the year left them
run_year <- function(model) {
  first <- run_pdm(model, year, initial_state(model, soil_fraction = 0.5))
  run_pdm(model, year, first$state)$output
}
to_m3s <- 20 / 3.6
```

All the runs below use the same rain: `r length(storm_days)` storms over `r n / 24` days, at
an hourly step. The first, 10 mm, falls on a dry catchment. Then come 20 mm, two 30 mm storms
two days apart, and 15 mm, as the catchment wets up. Potential evaporation is a steady
0.08 mm/h.

# 1. The soil store: how capacity is spread

## How it works

The PDM pictures the catchment as many small stores of different capacities, side by side.
Rain fills them all to the same depth, the *critical capacity*. Any store whose capacity is
below that depth is full, and every further drop of rain on it runs off. So the share of the
catchment producing runoff is the share of stores already full, and it grows as the catchment
wets up. The **capacity distribution** says how capacities are spread across the catchment,
and so how fast that contributing area grows.

```{r buckets, fig.height=3.2, fig.cap="Twenty stores drawn from each distribution, all with a mean capacity of 150 mm, filled to the same critical depth of 120 mm (dotted). Blue: water in stores not yet full. Orange: full stores, which shed any further rain as runoff. Tall outlines are cut off at the top of the panel."}
mean_c <- 150
cmax_for <- function(make) {
  stats::uniroot(function(cmax) capacity_mean(make(cmax)) - mean_c, c(mean_c, 10 * mean_c))$root
}
dists <- list(
  Pareto = FlodeParetoCapacity(0, cmax_for(function(x) FlodeParetoCapacity(0, x, 0.4)), 0.4),
  Rectangular = FlodeRectangularCapacity(0, 2 * mean_c),
  Triangular = FlodeTriangularCapacity(0, cmax_for(function(x) FlodeTriangularCapacity(0, x))),
  Exponential = FlodeExponentialCapacity(mean_c),
  Lognormal = FlodeLognormalCapacity(log(mean_c) - 0.5, 1)
)
quantile_of <- function(d, p) {
  vapply(p, function(pp) {
    stats::uniroot(function(c) capacity_cdf(d, c) - pp, c(0, 50 * mean_c))$root
  }, numeric(1))
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 5), mar = c(1, 0.5, 2, 0.5), cex.main = 0.9)
level <- 120
for (i in seq_along(dists)) {
  caps <- quantile_of(dists[[i]], (seq_len(20) - 0.5) / 20)
  top <- 450
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 20), ylim = c(0, top), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = names(dists)[i])
  for (j in seq_along(caps)) {
    h <- min(caps[j], top)
    full <- caps[j] <= level
    rect(j - 0.9, 0, j - 0.1, h, border = "#444444", col = NA)
    rect(j - 0.9, 0, j - 0.1, min(level, h),
         col = if (full) adjustcolor(pal[2], 0.7) else adjustcolor(pal[1], 0.5), border = NA)
  }
  abline(h = level, lty = 3, col = "#444444")
  text(10, top * 0.97, sprintf("%d of 20 full", sum(caps <= level)), cex = 0.8)
}
```

All five distributions hold the same water when full: 150 mm on average. They differ in the
spread:

- **Pareto** (the usual choice) has many shallow stores and few deep ones, up to a largest
  capacity, `cmax`. Its exponent `b` sets the spread: 0 means every store is the same size;
  larger values mean more shallow stores.
- **Rectangular** spreads capacities evenly from `cmin` to `cmax`.
- **Triangular** has most stores near the middle, with few very shallow or very deep.
- **Exponential** and **lognormal** have no largest store, and many very shallow ones, so part
  of the catchment runs off from the first rain.

## What it does to quick flow

```{r soil-runs}
soil_runs <- lapply(dists, function(d) {
  model <- pdm_model(distribution = d, area_km2 = 20)
  state <- initial_state(model, soil_fraction = 0.3)
  run_pdm(model, forcing, state)$output
})
```

```{r soil-storms, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Quick flow from one storm on the dry catchment (left, 10 mm on day 2) and one in the wet spell (right, 30 mm on day 15), each model starting with its soil 30 per cent full. Note the different scales."}
zoom <- function(day, title) {
  rows <- which(days >= day & days <= day + 1.5)
  hours <- (rows - rows[1])
  top <- max(sapply(soil_runs, function(o) max(o$surface_out_mm[rows])))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, max(hours)), ylim = c(0, top * 1.05), xlab = "Hours from the start of rain",
       ylab = "Quick flow (mm/h)", main = title, las = 1)
  for (i in seq_along(soil_runs)) {
    lines(hours, soil_runs[[i]]$surface_out_mm[rows], col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
  }
  peaks <- sapply(soil_runs, function(o) max(o$surface_out_mm[rows]))
  at <- hours[which.max(soil_runs[[1]]$surface_out_mm[rows])]
  end_labels(max(hours) * 1.02, peaks, sprintf("%s %.2f", names(soil_runs), peaks))
}
panels(right = 6.5)
zoom(2, "Dry catchment: 10 mm")
zoom(15, "Wet catchment: 30 mm")
```

The labels give each model's peak. On the dry catchment, the exponential and lognormal stores
give a clear response and the triangular almost none. By the wet spell every model responds
strongly, and the gap between them has narrowed.

```{r soil-cumulative, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Left: quick flow added up over the 40 days. Right: the share of the catchment producing runoff."}
panels(right = 6.5)
total <- sapply(soil_runs, function(o) cumsum(o$surface_out_mm))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 40), ylim = c(0, max(total)), xlab = "Day", ylab = "Quick flow so far (mm)",
     main = "Quick flow, added up", las = 1)
for (i in seq_along(soil_runs)) lines(days, total[, i], col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
end_labels(41, total[n, ], names(soil_runs))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 40), ylim = c(0, 0.7), xlab = "Day", ylab = "Share of catchment",
     main = "Contributing area", las = 1)
for (i in seq_along(soil_runs)) lines(days, soil_runs[[i]]$saturated_fraction, col = pal[i],
                                      lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
end_labels(41, sapply(soil_runs, function(o) o$saturated_fraction[n]), names(soil_runs))
```

```{r soil-ratios, fig.height=3.6, fig.cap="The share of each storm's rain that became direct runoff."}
storm_rows <- lapply(storm_days, function(d) which(days > d & days <= d + 1))
ratios <- sapply(soil_runs, function(o) {
  vapply(storm_rows, function(r) sum(o$direct_runoff_mm[r]) / sum(forcing$rain[r]), numeric(1))
})
par(mar = c(4.6, 5.2, 1, 0.8), mgp = c(3.6, 0.7, 0))
barplot(t(ratios), beside = TRUE, col = pal, border = NA, ylim = c(0, 1), las = 1,
        names.arg = sprintf("Day %d\n%g mm", storm_days, c(10, 20, 30, 30, 15)),
        ylab = "Direct runoff / rain")
legend("topleft", names(soil_runs), fill = pal, border = NA, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

The same storms, the same starting water, the same routing: only the spread of capacities
differs, yet the quick flow differs a lot.

- **The unbounded families respond most throughout.** Exponential and lognormal have many very
  shallow stores, so even the first small storm on a dry catchment runs off from about 30 per
  cent of it.
- **The bounded families depend most on wetness.** Their runoff ratio climbs steeply through the
  wet spell: the triangular distribution's rises six-fold from the first storm to the last, the
  exponential's less than two-fold. With few shallow stores, they shed little until the
  catchment has wetted up.

The panel below shows the same thing across the whole range of wetness. At any given soil
storage, the unbounded families shed more, and their share rises roughly in step with the
storage. The bounded families shed little until the store is well filled, then rise steeply
towards shedding everything as it nears full: a threshold-like response. The Pareto's `b` sets
how sharp that threshold is.

```{r soil-fill, fig.height=3.8, fig.cap="The share of 10 mm of rain that runs off at once, against how full the soil store is."}
fill_share <- seq(0, 0.995, length.out = 200)
par(mar = c(4.6, 5.2, 1, 0.8), mgp = c(3.6, 0.7, 0))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Soil store, share of its capacity",
     ylab = "Share of 10 mm that runs off", las = 1)
for (i in seq_along(dists)) {
  share <- vapply(fill_share, function(f) {
    soil_step(dists[[i]], f * capacity_mean(dists[[i]]), 10)$runoff / 10
  }, numeric(1))
  lines(fill_share, share, col = pal[i], lwd = 2, lty = i)
}
legend_in("topleft", names(dists))
```

## A year of storms, as an event table sees it

The short sequence shows the idea; a year of rain shows it as you would see it in a real record.
Each point below is one event found by `find_events()` in a year of simulated flow, placed by
how wet the soil was when its rain began and how much of the rain came back as quick flow.

```{r soil-year}
soil_year <- lapply(dists, function(d) run_year(pdm_model(distribution = d, area_km2 = 20)))
soil_events <- lapply(seq_along(dists), function(i) {
  o <- soil_year[[i]]
  ev <- find_events(year$rain, o$q_m3s, year$time, dt = 1, area_km2 = 20)
  ev <- ev[ev$rain_mm >= 5, ]
  data.frame(wet = o$soil_mm[ev$rain_start] / capacity_mean(dists[[i]]),
             ratio = ev$runoff_ratio)
})
```

```{r soil-scatter, fig.height=4.4, fig.cap="Every event of at least 5 mm in a year: its runoff ratio against the soil store's fill when its rain began. Lines: the median in bands of soil fill."}
par(mar = c(4.6, 5.2, 1, 6.5), mgp = c(3.6, 0.7, 0))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 0.8), xlab = "Soil store at the start of the rain, share of capacity",
     ylab = "Event runoff ratio", las = 1)
bands <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.1)
for (i in seq_along(soil_events)) {
  e <- soil_events[[i]]
  points(e$wet, e$ratio, col = adjustcolor(pal[i], 0.35), pch = 16, cex = 0.7)
  med <- tapply(e$ratio, cut(e$wet, bands), stats::median)
  mid <- bands[-1] - 0.05
  ok <- is.finite(med)
  lines(mid[ok], med[ok], col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
}
last <- sapply(soil_events, function(e) stats::median(e$ratio[e$wet > stats::quantile(e$wet, 0.8)]))
end_labels(1.01, last, names(dists))
```

In an observed record you can draw the same plot with the event table and a proxy for wetness,
such as the baseflow at the start of each event. A cloud that sits near zero until the soil is
half full, then climbs, points to a threshold-like store: Pareto with a small `b`, or
triangular. One that gives a clear ratio even from dry soil points to the exponential or
lognormal store, whose shallow stores fill first.

## The same water, different floods

A calibration that fits the total volume can still get the floods wrong. Below, each
distribution's capacities are scaled so that all five give exactly the same quick flow over
the year as the Pareto store. Their floods still differ.

```{r soil-equal}
scaled <- function(name, s) {
  switch(name,
    Pareto = FlodeParetoCapacity(0, dists$Pareto@cmax * s, 0.4),
    Rectangular = FlodeRectangularCapacity(0, dists$Rectangular@cmax * s),
    Triangular = FlodeTriangularCapacity(0, dists$Triangular@cmax * s),
    Exponential = FlodeExponentialCapacity(dists$Exponential@mean * s),
    Lognormal = FlodeLognormalCapacity(dists$Lognormal@meanlog + log(s), 1)
  )
}
quick_total <- function(d) sum(run_year(pdm_model(distribution = d, area_km2 = 20))$surface_out_mm)
target <- quick_total(dists$Pareto)
factors <- vapply(names(dists), function(nm) {
  if (nm == "Pareto") return(1)
  stats::uniroot(function(s) quick_total(scaled(nm, s)) - target, c(0.3, 6), tol = 1e-4)$root
}, numeric(1))
equal_runs <- lapply(names(dists), function(nm) {
  run_year(pdm_model(distribution = scaled(nm, factors[[nm]]), area_km2 = 20))
})
names(equal_runs) <- names(dists)
floods <- find_events(year$rain, equal_runs$Pareto$q_m3s, year$time, dt = 1, area_km2 = 20)
floods <- floods[order(floods$peak_flow, decreasing = TRUE)[1:6], ]
peaks <- sapply(equal_runs, function(o) {
  vapply(seq_len(nrow(floods)), function(k) {
    max(o$q_m3s[floods$flow_start[k]:floods$flow_end[k]])
  }, numeric(1))
})
```

```{r soil-equal-plot, fig.height=4, fig.cap="The six largest floods of the year, with every distribution scaled to give the same total quick flow. Each line is one distribution; the storms are in date order."}
order_date <- order(floods$flow_start)
par(mar = c(4.6, 5.2, 1, 6.5), mgp = c(3.6, 0.7, 0))
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 6), ylim = range(peaks), xaxt = "n", xlab = "", las = 1,
     ylab = "Flood peak (m3/s)")
axis(1, at = 1:6, labels = format(floods$rain_start_time[order_date], "%d %b"), cex.axis = 0.85)
for (i in seq_along(equal_runs)) {
  lines(1:6, peaks[order_date, i], col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i, type = "b", pch = 16)
}
end_labels(6.1, peaks[order_date[6], ], names(equal_runs))
```

```{r soil-equal-numbers, include=FALSE}
spread <- apply(peaks, 1, function(x) (max(x) - min(x)) / mean(x))
```

With the same year's quick flow, the flood peaks still differ by up to
`r round(100 * max(spread))` per cent between distributions, in a pattern that changes from
storm to storm with how wet the catchment was. The scaling needed was large: the exponential
store's mean capacity had to change by a factor of `r sprintf("%.2f", factors[["Exponential"]])`
to match. Volume alone cannot choose the distribution; the floods can.

> **What to look for.** Compare the runoff ratios of similar storms in dry and wet conditions,
> using `find_events()` and the event table. Small dry-weather storms giving a clear response,
> and a ratio that rises steadily with wetness, point to many shallow stores: a larger Pareto
> `b`, or the exponential or lognormal distribution. Little response until the catchment is
> wet, then a sharp rise, points to a threshold-like store: a smaller Pareto `b`, or the
> triangular distribution.

# 2. Recharge: how water reaches groundwater

## How it works

Recharge decides how much water goes to the slow groundwater route rather than the quick
surface route, and when.

- **Standard** recharge drains the soil store downward, at a rate that grows with how full it
  is: `d = (S - St)^bg / kg`. Recharge goes on between storms, as long as the soil holds water
  above the tension threshold `St`.
- **Split** recharge takes nothing from the soil store. A fixed share, `1 - alpha`, of each
  storm's direct runoff goes to groundwater, and the rest to the surface. Recharge happens only
  while it is running off.
- **Demand** recharge drains the soil according to how much room the groundwater store has:
  fast when groundwater is low, slowing as it fills.

```{r recharge-diagram, fig.height=2.8, fig.cap="Where each rule takes groundwater recharge from."}
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0), cex.main = 0.95)
draw_rule <- function(title, from_soil, from_runoff, note) {
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "", main = title)
  box_at(0.5, 0.82, 0.5, 0.18, "Soil store", pal[1], cex = 0.85)
  box_at(0.22, 0.4, 0.34, 0.16, "Surface", grey, cex = 0.85)
  box_at(0.75, 0.4, 0.4, 0.16, "Groundwater", pal[3], cex = 0.85)
  arrow(0.4, 0.73, 0.27, 0.48)
  text(0.17, 0.62, "runoff", cex = 0.75)
  if (from_soil) arrow(0.62, 0.73, 0.74, 0.48, col = pal[2])
  if (from_runoff) arrow(0.27, 0.32, 0.6, 0.36, col = pal[2])
  text(0.5, 0.12, note, cex = 0.78)
}
draw_rule("Standard", TRUE, FALSE, "drains the soil, between\nstorms as well as during them")
draw_rule("Split", FALSE, TRUE, "a share of runoff,\nonly while it runs off")
draw_rule("Demand", TRUE, FALSE, "drains the soil, faster when\ngroundwater has room")
```

```{r recharge-runs}
rules <- list(
  Standard = FlodeStandardRecharge(kg = 400, bg = 1, st = 0),
  Split = FlodeSplitRecharge(alpha = 0.5),
  Demand = FlodeDemandRecharge(alpha = 0.5, beta = 1.5, qsat = 0.3)
)
# Each model starts in steady state at the same flow, 0.2 m3/s, 70 per cent of it baseflow
recharge_runs <- lapply(rules, function(r) {
  model <- pdm_model(recharge = r, groundwater = cubic_routing(kb = 20000), area_km2 = 20)
  state <- suppressWarnings(initial_state_from_flow(model, observed_m3s = 0.2,
                                                    baseflow_fraction = 0.7, soil_fraction = 0.6))
  run_pdm(model, forcing, state)$output
})
```

```{r recharge-plots, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Left: recharge to groundwater added up over the 40 days; grey bands mark the storms. Right: the baseflow it produces. Every model starts in steady state at the same flow."}
panels(right = 5.5)
cum <- sapply(recharge_runs, function(o) cumsum(o$groundwater_input_mm))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 40), ylim = c(0, max(cum)), xlab = "Day", ylab = "Recharge so far (mm)",
     main = "Recharge, added up", las = 1)
for (d in storm_days) rect(d, 0, d + 0.4, max(cum), col = adjustcolor(grey, 0.35), border = NA)
for (i in seq_along(recharge_runs)) lines(days, cum[, i], col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
end_labels(41, cum[n, ], names(recharge_runs))
base <- sapply(recharge_runs, function(o) o$baseflow_out_mm)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 40), ylim = c(0, max(base)), xlab = "Day", ylab = "Baseflow (mm/h)",
     main = "Baseflow", las = 1)
for (d in storm_days) rect(d, 0, d + 0.4, max(base), col = adjustcolor(grey, 0.35), border = NA)
for (i in seq_along(recharge_runs)) lines(days, base[, i], col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
end_labels(41, base[n, ], names(recharge_runs))
```

In the cumulative plot, a line that climbs only in steps, at the storms, is recharge from
runoff; a line that keeps climbing between storms is drainage from the soil.

```{r recharge-fate}
fate <- t(sapply(recharge_runs, function(o) {
  c(evaporation = sum(o$aet_mm), quick = sum(o$surface_out_mm), slow = sum(o$baseflow_out_mm))
}))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  rule = rownames(fate), evaporation_mm = round(fate[, "evaporation"]),
  quick_flow_mm = round(fate[, "quick"]), slow_flow_mm = round(fate[, "slow"]),
  slow_share = round(fate[, "slow"] / (fate[, "quick"] + fate[, "slow"]), 2)
), row.names = FALSE, caption = paste("Over the 40 days and", sum(forcing$rain), "mm of rain:",
                                      "where the water went, and the slow route's share of the",
                                      "river's flow."))
```

- **Standard** recharge carries on after each storm, draining the soil for days, so baseflow
  rises slowly, peaks after the rain has stopped and falls slowly. Most of the water reaches the
  river by the slow route.
- **Split** recharge comes in pulses, only while the catchment runs off. Baseflow jumps with
  each storm and recedes at once. Nothing drains from the soil between storms, so more of the
  rain is held there and evaporates, and the slow route carries about half the flow.
- **Demand** recharge drains the soil hard while groundwater has room: bursts during each storm,
  then a steady rate of up to `qsat` between them. Baseflow is held high and flat, then
  collapses once the soil can no longer supply it. Little water stays in the soil long enough
  to evaporate.

The amounts depend on the parameter values chosen here; the shapes are what each rule gives.

## Through a year: low flows and the seasons

Forty days of storms cannot show how each rule carries the river through summer. A year can.

```{r recharge-year}
recharge_year <- lapply(rules, function(r) {
  run_year(pdm_model(recharge = r, groundwater = cubic_routing(kb = 20000), area_km2 = 20))
})
```

```{r recharge-fdc, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Left: flow duration curves over the year, every flow ranked from highest to lowest, on a log scale; dotted lines mark Q70 and Q95. Right: the baseflow index by month, the slow route's share of each month's flow."}
panels(right = 5.5)
exceed <- (seq_len(ny) - 0.5) / ny * 100
fdc <- sapply(recharge_year, function(o) sort(o$q_m3s, decreasing = TRUE))
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 100), ylim = range(fdc[fdc > 0]), log = "y", las = 1,
     xlab = "Share of time flow is exceeded (%)", ylab = "Flow (m3/s, log scale)",
     main = "Flow duration curves")
abline(v = c(70, 95), col = grey, lty = 3)
for (i in seq_along(recharge_year)) lines(exceed, fdc[, i], col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
end_labels(101, fdc[ny, ], names(recharge_year), log_y = TRUE)
month <- factor(format(year$time, "%b"), levels = month.abb[c(10:12, 1:9)])
bfi <- sapply(recharge_year, function(o) {
  tapply(o$baseflow_out_mm, month, sum) / tapply(o$baseflow_out_mm + o$surface_out_mm, month, sum)
})
par(mar = c(4.6, 4.6, 2.2, 0.8))
barplot(t(bfi), beside = TRUE, col = pal[1:3], border = NA, ylim = c(0, 1.2), las = 2,
        yaxt = "n", ylab = "Baseflow index", main = "Baseflow index by month", cex.names = 0.8)
axis(2, at = seq(0, 1, 0.2), las = 1)
legend("top", names(recharge_year), fill = pal[1:3], border = NA, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE,
       cex = 0.8)
```

```{r recharge-year-numbers, include=FALSE}
q95 <- apply(fdc, 2, function(x) x[ceiling(0.95 * ny)])
```

The rules part company at the low-flow end of the duration curve, where the river is fed only
by groundwater. Q95, the flow exceeded 95 per cent of the time, is
`r sprintf("%.3f", q95[["Standard"]])` m3/s with standard recharge,
`r sprintf("%.3f", q95[["Split"]])` with split and `r sprintf("%.3f", q95[["Demand"]])` with
demand. Standard recharge keeps groundwater fed from the soil into summer; split recharge
starves it once storms stop running off. Demand recharge gives the highest flows for most of the
year but falls away in late summer, once the soil it draws on is dry.

The monthly baseflow index tells the rules apart at once, but hardly changes with the season:
about half the flow under split recharge, more than nine-tenths under standard, nearly all
under demand. Each rule fixes the share; the season sets only how much water there is to
share.

> **What to look for.** Watch how baseflow behaves after a storm. Baseflow that keeps rising for
> days after the rain has stopped, then falls slowly, is soil drainage: standard recharge.
> Baseflow that steps up during each storm and starts falling at once points to split recharge.
> Baseflow held high and flat through a wet spell, then dropping away, points to demand
> recharge. The baseflow index, from `water_balance()`, says how large the slow route must be.

# 3. The groundwater store: how it drains

## How it works

The groundwater store turns recharge into baseflow through a storage-outflow relationship. In
a **linear** store the outflow is proportional to the storage, `q = S / kb`. In **quadratic**
and **cubic** stores it rises with the square or the cube of the storage, `q = S^m / kb`, so a
full store drains fast and a nearly empty one very slowly. In the **exponential** store, outflow
grows exponentially with storage, giving the slowest tail of all.

To compare them fairly, every store below starts draining at the same rate, 0.01 mm/h, takes
the same steady input, 0.1 mm/h, and holds the same 60 mm more water at its equilibrium than
at the start. They differ only in how outflow depends on storage in between.

```{r stores}
q_start <- 0.01
q0 <- 0.1
active <- 60
k_for <- function(m) (active / (q0^(1 / m) - q_start^(1 / m)))^m
a <- log(q0 / q_start) / active
stores <- list(
  Linear = linear_routing(kb = k_for(1)),
  Quadratic = quadratic_routing(kb = k_for(2)),
  Cubic = cubic_routing(kb = k_for(3)),
  Exponential = FlodeExponentialRouting(a = a, gamma = log(q0) - a * 100)
)
route_series <- function(r, inflow, s) {
  q <- numeric(length(inflow))
  for (i in seq_along(inflow)) {
    step <- route_step(r, s, inflow[i], 1)
    s <- step$storage
    q[i] <- step$q_end
  }
  q
}
```

```{r stores-fill, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="The same input to every store: 0.1 mm/h for 60 days, starting from an outflow of 0.01 mm/h, then nothing for 60 days. Left: outflow. Right: each store's outflow as a share of the linear store's, which shows where they differ."}
hours <- 24 * 120
inflow <- c(rep(q0, 24 * 60), rep(0, 24 * 60))
fill <- lapply(stores, function(r) route_series(r, inflow, storage_for_flow(r, q_start)))
t_days <- seq_len(hours) / 24
panels(right = 6.5)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 120), ylim = c(0, q0 * 1.05), xlab = "Day", ylab = "Outflow (mm/h)",
     main = "Filling and draining", las = 1)
abline(h = q0, col = grey, lty = 3)
abline(v = 60, col = grey, lty = 3)
for (i in seq_along(fill)) lines(t_days, fill[[i]], col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
end_labels(122, sapply(fill, function(q) q[length(q)]), names(fill))
ratio <- lapply(fill, function(q) q / fill$Linear)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 120), ylim = range(unlist(ratio)), xlab = "Day",
     ylab = "Outflow / linear store's", main = "Compared with the linear store", las = 1)
abline(h = 1, col = pal[1], lwd = 2.5)
abline(v = 60, col = grey, lty = 3)
for (i in 2:4) lines(t_days, ratio[[i]], col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
end_labels(122, sapply(ratio, function(r) r[length(r)]), names(fill))
```

Given the same water to fill, the four stores behave much alike: the store's form changes the
shape of the response, not its size. The right-hand panel shows where they differ:

- **Filling.** The nonlinear stores lag at first, giving 25 to 40 per cent less outflow than
  the linear store in the first weeks, then catch up and overtake it as they near the input
  rate: an S-shaped rise, against the linear store's steady approach.
- **Draining.** When input stops, the nonlinear stores fall faster at first, then flatten.
  After about 40 days they give more flow than the linear store, and the gap keeps growing:
  the long tail that the next section explains.

## Recession curves: the store's fingerprint

### What a recession curve is

After rain stops and the quick flow has passed, the river is fed only by the groundwater
store draining. That falling limb is the **recession**. How fast the flow falls depends on how
much water is left, and the form of the store sets that relationship. A recession curve
measures it: for every point on a recession, the **rate of fall** (how many mm/h the flow drops
per hour, `-dQ/dt`) against the **flow** at that moment (`Q`).

```{r recession-explainer, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="From hydrograph to recession curve. Left: a recession, with the slope of the hydrograph (the rate of fall) marked at three points. Right: the same three points as rate of fall against flow, on log scales. Every point of every recession goes on the right-hand plot."}
r <- cubic_routing(kb = 3.375e7)
q_ex <- route_series(r, rep(0, 24 * 90), storage_for_flow(r, 0.1))
d_ex <- seq_along(q_ex) / 24
marks <- c(5, 25, 70)
panels()
plot(d_ex, q_ex, type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = pal[1], xlab = "Day", ylab = "Flow Q (mm/h)",
     main = "A recession", las = 1, ylim = c(0, 0.1))
fall_at <- function(day) {
  i <- which.min(abs(d_ex - day))
  c(q = q_ex[i], fall = q_ex[i - 1] - q_ex[i])
}
for (k in seq_along(marks)) {
  p <- fall_at(marks[k])
  span <- 12
  segments(marks[k] - span, p[["q"]] + p[["fall"]] * 24 * span,
           marks[k] + span, p[["q"]] - p[["fall"]] * 24 * span, col = pal[2], lwd = 2)
  points(marks[k], p[["q"]], pch = 19, col = pal[2])
  text(marks[k], p[["q"]], LETTERS[k], pos = 3, offset = 0.8, font = 2)
}
mid <- (q_ex[-1] + q_ex[-length(q_ex)]) / 2
plot(mid, -diff(q_ex), log = "xy", type = "l", lwd = 2.5, col = pal[1], las = 1,
     xlab = "Flow Q (mm/h)", ylab = "Rate of fall -dQ/dt (mm/h per h)", main = "Its recession curve")
for (k in seq_along(marks)) {
  p <- fall_at(marks[k])
  points(p[["q"]], p[["fall"]], pch = 19, col = pal[2])
  text(p[["q"]], p[["fall"]], LETTERS[k], pos = 3, offset = 0.8, font = 2)
}
```

Early in the recession (A) the flow is high and falls fast; later (B, C) it is lower and falls
more slowly. On log scales, the points line up along a straight line. That line is the
recession curve.

### How to read it

- **The slope is the store's form.** The steeper the line, the more the rate of fall slows as
  the flow drops. A linear store gives a slope of 1: the flow always loses the same share of
  itself per day, so it halves in the same time whatever its level. Nonlinear stores give
  steeper slopes, 1.5 for the quadratic, 5/3 for the cubic and 2 for the exponential: the
  lower the flow, the longer it takes to halve, and the recession tails off.
- **The height is the store's size.** At a given flow, a line higher up means a faster fall:
  a smaller or quicker store. Flow divided by its rate of fall is the store's response time at
  that flow, in hours. For a linear store it is the same at every flow; for a nonlinear store
  it grows as the flow falls.

The difference between the stores is clearest if they start alike. Below, all four start at
the same flow, 0.1 mm/h, falling at the same rate (a response time of 500 hours), and drain
with no more input.

```{r recession-compare, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Four stores starting at the same flow and the same rate of fall, draining for 120 days. Left: the recessions on a log scale. Right: their recession curves, with the slopes the store forms predict (dashed)."}
tau <- 500
tangent <- list(
  Linear = linear_routing(kb = q0 * tau / q0),
  Quadratic = quadratic_routing(kb = (2 * q0 * tau)^2 / q0),
  Cubic = cubic_routing(kb = (3 * q0 * tau)^3 / q0),
  Exponential = FlodeExponentialRouting(a = 1 / (q0 * tau), gamma = log(q0))
)
drain <- lapply(tangent, function(r) route_series(r, rep(0, 24 * 120), storage_for_flow(r, q0)))
t_drain <- seq_len(24 * 120) / 24
panels(right = 6.5)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 120), ylim = c(2e-4, q0), log = "y", xlab = "Day",
     ylab = "Flow (mm/h, log scale)", main = "Recessions from the same start", las = 1)
for (i in seq_along(drain)) lines(t_drain, drain[[i]], col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
end_labels(122, sapply(drain, function(q) q[length(q)]), names(drain), log_y = TRUE)
slopes <- c(1, 1.5, 5 / 3, 2)
plot(NA, xlim = c(2e-4, q0), ylim = c(1e-8, 1e-3), log = "xy", xlab = "Flow Q (mm/h)",
     ylab = "Rate of fall -dQ/dt (mm/h per h)", main = "Recession curves", las = 1)
for (i in seq_along(drain)) {
  q <- drain[[i]]
  fall <- -diff(q)
  mid <- (q[-1] + q[-length(q)]) / 2
  lines(mid, fall, col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5, lty = i)
  qq <- c(2e-4, q0)
  lines(qq, fall[1] * (qq / mid[1])^slopes[i], col = adjustcolor(pal[i], 0.6), lty = 2)
}
legend("bottomright", sprintf("%s, slope %s", names(drain), c("1", "1.5", "5/3", "2")),
       col = pal, lty = 1:4, lwd = 2.5, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
```

From the same start, after 120 days the linear store is down to
`r sprintf("%.4f", drain$Linear[length(drain$Linear)])` mm/h, while the cubic still gives
`r sprintf("%.4f", drain$Cubic[length(drain$Cubic)])` mm/h and the exponential
`r sprintf("%.4f", drain$Exponential[length(drain$Exponential)])` mm/h: thirty to fifty times
more.
That is the difference between a river that dries to a trickle in a long summer and one that
keeps flowing.

### Halving time: the recession in days

The recession curve says the same thing in a form that is easy to picture: **how long the flow
takes to halve**, at each flow. A linear store takes the same time whatever the flow. A
nonlinear store takes longer and longer as the flow falls.

```{r halving, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="How many days each store's flow takes to halve, at each flow, from the recessions above. Flow on a log scale."}
par(mar = c(4.6, 5.2, 1, 6.5), mgp = c(3.6, 0.7, 0))
halving <- lapply(drain, function(q) {
  mid <- (q[-1] + q[-length(q)]) / 2
  list(q = mid, days = log(2) * mid / (-diff(q)) / 24)
})
plot(NA, xlim = c(3e-4, q0), ylim = c(0, max(sapply(halving, function(h) max(h$days)))),
     log = "x", las = 1, xlab = "Flow Q (mm/h, log scale)", ylab = "Days to halve")
for (i in seq_along(halving)) lines(halving[[i]]$q, halving[[i]]$days, col = pal[i], lwd = 2.5,
                                    lty = i)
end_labels(q0 * 1.05, sapply(halving, function(h) h$days[1]), names(halving))
```

All four start at about `r round(halving$Linear$days[1])` days to halve. The linear store stays
there. By the end of its recession the cubic store takes
`r round(max(halving$Cubic$days))` days and the exponential
`r round(max(halving$Exponential$days))`. Staff can read halving times straight off a log-scale
hydrograph: a recession that halves every two weeks in March and every two months in September
is a nonlinear store.

### Recessions after small and large floods

A quick test on an observed record: lay the recessions after floods of different sizes over
each other, each scaled by its starting flow. A linear store gives the same curve every time.
A nonlinear store falls faster, at first, after a large flood than after a small one.

```{r small-large, fig.height=4.2, fig.cap="Recessions from three starting flows, each divided by its starting flow. Left: the linear store, whose recessions coincide. Right: the cubic store, whose recession after the largest flood falls fastest."}
starts <- c(Large = 0.1, Medium = 0.03, Small = 0.01)
panels(right = 5.5)
for (nm in c("Linear", "Cubic")) {
  r <- tangent[[nm]]
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 60), ylim = c(0.05, 1), log = "y", las = 1, xlab = "Days since the start",
       ylab = "Flow / starting flow (log scale)", main = paste(nm, "store"))
  ends <- numeric(0)
  for (k in seq_along(starts)) {
    q <- route_series(r, rep(0, 24 * 60), storage_for_flow(r, starts[k]))
    lines(seq_along(q) / 24, q / starts[k], col = pal[k], lwd = 2.5, lty = k)
    ends <- c(ends, q[length(q)] / starts[k])
  }
  end_labels(61, ends, names(starts), log_y = TRUE)
}
```

### Recession curves from a real river

`recession_analysis()` builds the recession curve from an observed record, and
`plot_recession()` draws it with a fitted model's alongside:

```{r recession-usage, echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
rec <- recession_analysis(flow, rain, dt = 0.25, time = time, months = c(11:12, 1:3))
rec
plot(rec)
```

A real record is noisier than these curves, and five things shape it:

1. **Only true recessions count.** Points where rain fell, or soon after it while the quick
   flow is still passing, are not the groundwater store draining. The function uses only
   falling flow, some time after the last rain (three response times by default).
2. **Average the flow first.** At 15-minute steps the rate of fall is mostly noise; the function
   averages to daily flow by default.
3. **Recharge between storms flattens the slope.** With standard recharge, the soil keeps feeding
   groundwater through a recession, so the flow falls more slowly than the store alone would
   make it, and the slope reads low. On made-up catchments the slope read 0.1 to 0.9 too low.
   Read the store's form straight from the slope only where recharge stops between storms.
4. **Evaporation steepens summer recessions.** Winter recessions, `months = c(11:12, 1:3)` above,
   show the store more cleanly.
5. **The slope is a check, not the choice.** In a benchmark of sixteen made-up catchments, the
   slope found the true store in eight. Use it to check that a fitted model's low flows fall at
   the right rate, and let the structure comparison choose the store.

> **What to look for.** Plot the winter dry-weather recessions on a log scale. A straight line,
> the flow halving in the same number of days whatever its level, points to a linear store. A
> recession that falls fast from high flow and then flattens into a long tail points to a
> nonlinear store: cubic for most UK catchments with groundwater, exponential if the tail barely
> falls through a long dry spell. `plot_recession()` then shows whether the fitted model's
> recessions match the river's.

# Fingerprints

The same measures for every option, each changed one at a time from a common model and run
over the same year. These are measures you can take from an observed record, so the table is a
guide to which option a river resembles.

```{r fingerprints}
base_d <- dists$Pareto
base_r <- FlodeStandardRecharge(kg = 400, bg = 1, st = 0)
base_g <- tangent$Cubic
variants <- c(
  lapply(dists, function(d) list(d = d, r = base_r, g = base_g)),
  lapply(rules, function(r) list(d = base_d, r = r, g = base_g)),
  lapply(tangent, function(g) list(d = base_d, r = base_r, g = g))
)
group <- rep(c("Soil store", "Recharge", "Groundwater"),
             c(length(dists), length(rules), length(tangent)))
day <- as.Date(year$time)
daily_rain <- tapply(year$rain, day, sum)
measure <- function(o) {
  q <- o$q_m3s
  dq <- tapply(q, day, mean)
  dry <- stats::filter(daily_rain < 0.5, rep(1, 4), sides = 1) == 4
  falling <- c(FALSE, diff(dq) < 0)
  use <- which(dry & falling)
  half <- log(2) * dq[use] / (dq[use - 1] - dq[use])
  c(flow_mm = sum(q) * 3.6 / 20, peak_m3s = max(q),
    bfi = sum(o$baseflow_out_mm) / sum(o$baseflow_out_mm + o$surface_out_mm),
    q95_q50 = unname(stats::quantile(q, 0.05) / stats::quantile(q, 0.5)),
    halving_days = stats::median(half, na.rm = TRUE))
}
prints <- t(sapply(variants, function(v) {
  measure(run_year(pdm_model(distribution = v$d, recharge = v$r, groundwater = v$g,
                             area_km2 = 20)))
}))
```

```{r fingerprint-table}
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  component = group, option = rownames(prints),
  annual_flow_mm = round(prints[, "flow_mm"]), peak_m3s = round(prints[, "peak_m3s"], 2),
  baseflow_index = round(prints[, "bfi"], 2), q95_over_q50 = round(prints[, "q95_q50"], 2),
  dry_halving_days = round(prints[, "halving_days"], 1)
), row.names = FALSE, caption = paste(
  "One option changed at a time from a common model (Pareto soil store, standard recharge,",
  "cubic groundwater store), over the same year. Q95/Q50 is the low-flow index: higher means",
  "better-sustained low flows. Dry halving time is the median days to halve on falling days",
  "after four dry days."))
```

Read the table by column. The soil store options differ most in the peak; the recharge rules
in the baseflow index and the low-flow index; the groundwater stores in the low-flow index and
the dry-weather halving time. That is where to look in a record for each choice.

The recharge rules also change the annual flow, from `r round(prints["Split", "flow_mm"])` mm
with split recharge to `r round(prints["Demand", "flow_mm"])` mm with demand. Water left in the
soil store evaporates; water sent on to groundwater does not. So the rule decides the water
balance as well as the shape of the hydrograph, and a model that runs short of water year
after year may have the wrong rule rather than the wrong rain.

# Putting it together

The table gathers what to look for, and how to represent it.

| What you see in the record | What it points to | How to represent it |
|---|---|---|
| Small storms on a dry catchment give a clear response | many shallow stores | larger Pareto `b`, or the exponential distribution |
| Little response until the catchment is wet, then most rain runs off | a threshold-like store | smaller Pareto `b`, or triangular |
| The runoff ratio rises steadily with wetness | capacities spread widely | exponential or lognormal distribution |
| Baseflow keeps rising for days after rain stops | soil drainage to groundwater | standard recharge, with `kg` setting the pace |
| Baseflow steps up during storms and falls at once | recharge from runoff only | split recharge, with `alpha` the surface share |
| Baseflow held high and flat through a wet spell, then dropping away | recharge driven by groundwater room | demand recharge |
| Recessions are straight lines on a log scale | a linear store | linear groundwater store |
| Recessions fall fast, then flatten into a long tail | a nonlinear store | cubic store (or quadratic) |
| A tail that barely falls through a dry summer | a very slow, deep store | exponential store |
| Tiny event runoff ratios, yet a large and steady river | water reaching the river by the slow route | standard recharge from a threshold-like soil store |
| Each storm lifts the whole flow, with little separate spike | recharge almost as fast as runoff | demand recharge |
| The model runs short of water year after year, with good shapes | water left in the soil and evaporated | a recharge rule that sends more water on, once the rain and the area are checked |
| A sharp spike on top of a slower flood hydrograph | two quick timescales | a two-zone model ([The two-zone PDM](two-zone-pdm.html)) |

Three cautions:

1. **The options trade off.** A larger `cmax` and a smaller `b` can give similar runoff, and so
   can several recharge settings. Look at the record to decide which family is plausible, and
   let calibration choose within it.
2. **Check the data before the structure.** Flow higher than the rain can explain, or a storm
   the river barely felt, is more often a data problem than a missing component. See
   [Checking the data and the events](checks.html).
3. **The structure recommendation does this comparison for you,** on validation data, and the
   report shows why it chose each component. Use this article to judge whether its choice makes
   sense for the river you know. See [How the model structure is chosen](choosing-structure.html).

# Exercises: mystery hydrographs

Each record below was made by a model with one option from each component. The options are not
named. Use the clues in this article to work out which, then open the answer.

```{r mysteries}
mysteries <- list(
  A = list(d = dists$Exponential, r = FlodeSplitRecharge(alpha = 0.5), g = tangent$Linear),
  B = list(d = FlodeParetoCapacity(0, 165, 0.1), r = base_r, g = base_g),
  C = list(d = dists$Rectangular, r = FlodeDemandRecharge(alpha = 0.5, beta = 1.5, qsat = 0.3),
           g = tangent$Exponential)
)
mystery_runs <- lapply(mysteries, function(v) {
  run_year(pdm_model(distribution = v$d, recharge = v$r, groundwater = v$g, area_km2 = 20))
})
draw_mystery <- function(o, label) {
  panels(right = 2)
  q <- o$q_m3s
  plot(year$time, q, type = "l", log = "y", col = pal[1], lwd = 1.2, las = 1,
       xlab = "", ylab = "Flow (m3/s, log scale)", main = paste0("Mystery ", label, ": the year"))
  ev <- find_events(year$rain, q, year$time, dt = 1, area_km2 = 20)
  ev <- ev[ev$rain_mm >= 5, ]
  plot(ev$rain_start_time, ev$runoff_ratio, pch = 16, col = pal[2], las = 1, ylim = c(0, 1),
       xlab = "", ylab = "Event runoff ratio", main = "Its events")
}
```

**Mystery A**

```{r mystery-a, fig.height=4}
draw_mystery(mystery_runs$A, "A")
```

1. Do small storms on a dry catchment give a response?
2. After a storm, does baseflow keep rising, or fall at once?
3. On the log scale, are the dry-weather recessions straight or curved?

<details><summary>Answer A</summary>

An **exponential** soil store, **split** recharge and a **linear** groundwater store. Every event
returns a share of its rain, even in a dry summer: many shallow stores. The flow drops back
after each storm with no slow rise between them: recharge only from runoff. The recessions are
straight on the log scale, halving in the same time at any level: a linear store.

</details>

**Mystery B**

```{r mystery-b, fig.height=4}
draw_mystery(mystery_runs$B, "B")
```

1. How much of each storm's rain comes back as quick flow?
2. Yet how large is the flow, and what shape does it take through the year?

<details><summary>Answer B</summary>

A **Pareto store with a small `b`** (0.1), **standard** recharge and a **cubic** groundwater store.
Storms return almost nothing as quick flow, in winter as in summer: a threshold-like store that
sheds little until it is nearly full, and standard recharge drains it before it fills. Yet the
river is never low. The water reaches it by the slow route, so the flow swells and shrinks in
smooth arcs over weeks: soil drainage into a nonlinear store. A chalk or sandstone river looks
like this.

</details>

**Mystery C**

```{r mystery-c, fig.height=4}
draw_mystery(mystery_runs$C, "C")
```

1. Does each storm give a sharp spike, or lift the whole flow?
2. Compare how fast the flow falls after a rise with how fast it falls in late summer.

<details><summary>Answer C</summary>

A **rectangular** soil store, **demand** recharge and an **exponential** groundwater store. Each
storm lifts the whole flow, with little of a separate spike: demand recharge pulls water from
the soil whenever groundwater has room, so it reaches the river by the slow route almost as fast
as runoff. Few storms count as events, and their ratios are low and scattered. A high rise
halves in two or three weeks; the late-summer recession, from a lower flow, takes about twice
as long: an exponential store, quicker when full and slower when low.

</details>
